quote: we recorded $347 million of a reach-forward loss due to a reduction in projected delivery price increases associated with escalation and an increase in estimated costs due to our decisions to reduce twin-aisle production rates which impact production rates beginning in 2010.
finding: Boeing cut twin-aisle rates in the 2008-09 recession and took a $347M 747 loss partly because of those cuts.
trigger: 2008-09 recession and weak widebody demand
response: Reduced twin-aisle production rates from 2010

quote: In April 2009, we announced a delay in previous plans to increase the production rate. ... In April 2009, we announced that we will lower the production rate on our 777 airplane program, affecting deliveries beginning in June 2010.
finding: In April 2009 Boeing responded to the downturn by delaying a planned 767 rate increase and cutting the 777 rate (7 to 5 per month from June 2010).
trigger: Global recession and airline losses 2008-09
response: 767 rate increase delayed; 777 rate cut
lag: announced about a year before taking effect

quote: On July 30, 2009, we acquired the business, assets and operations of Vought Aircraft Industries, Inc.’s (Vought) 787 business conducted at North Charleston, South Carolina. ... On December 22, 2009, we acquired Alenia North America’s 50% ownership interest in Global Aeronautica.
finding: Faced with 787 supplier failures, Boeing bought its struggling fuselage suppliers (Vought's Charleston plant and full control of Global Aeronautica).
trigger: 787 supply-chain and workmanship problems
response: Acquired Vought 787 operations and Global Aeronautica

quote: On October 28, 2009 we announced the North Charleston facility as the location for a second final assembly site for the 787 Dreamliner program. ... Until the additional 787 assembly line is fully operational, we will establish transitional surge capability at our Everett, Washington, location
finding: Boeing committed capital to a second 787 final-assembly line (Charleston) plus a temporary Everett surge line to raise rates.

quote: We believe our ability to access external capital resources should be sufficient to satisfy existing short-term and long-term commitments and plans, and also to provide adequate financial flexibility to take advantage of potential strategic business opportunities should they arise within the next year.
finding: Boeing kept debt capacity in reserve to take up strategic opportunities, an opportunistic balance-sheet stance.

quote: We do not commit to industrial participation agreements unless a contract for sale of our products or services is signed. ... As of December 31, 2009, we have outstanding industrial participation agreements totaling $11 billion that extend through 2024.
finding: Boeing uses industrial-participation offsets ($11B outstanding) to win foreign sales, but commits only once a sale is signed.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: before the end of this year, Heidi, on the narrow body, we'll have charted a course of either re-engining or moving onto the new airplane.
finding: Faced with a likely Airbus geared-turbofan re-engine, Boeing committed to choose re-engine or new airplane within 2010.
trigger: Prospect of Airbus announcing a GTF-powered A320 re-engine in 2010
response: Decide narrowbody course (re-engine vs new airplane) by end of 2010

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: The improving market conditions and the disciplined approach we have taken in managing production rates are paying off. As we announced last month, we have accelerated plans to increase production rates on both the 777 and the 747-8.
finding: Early in the recovery Boeing brought forward planned 777 and 747-8 rate increases, crediting its disciplined rate management through the downturn.
trigger: Recovering air traffic and customer accelerations in early 2010
response: Accelerated 777 and 747-8 rate increases

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we expect to be at a total production rate of 10 787s per month by the end of 2013. Anticipating three per month will be assembled at our expanded Boeing Charleston Facility
finding: Boeing planned a 10/month 787 rate by end-2013, with a second final assembly line in Charleston producing 3/month.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: First of all, we wouldn't increase the rate unless we had a pretty visible look at demand.
finding: Boeing raises rates only with clear demand visibility.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: the kind of improvements we think we can make in the 777, both the smaller and larger versions, may be enough to handle the old -10 mission between the two of them. We're not sure yet but that question is something that we're debating and modeling right now.
finding: Boeing weighed whether an upgraded 777 plus the 787-9 could make the 787-10 unnecessary, trading off widebody derivatives.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I think before the end of this year, Heidi, on the narrow body, we'll have charted a course of either re-engining or moving onto the new airplane.
finding: Asked how it would answer an Airbus GTF re-engine, Boeing promised a re-engine-or-new-airplane decision by end-2010; by January 2011 it was still leaning new and studying through 2011.
trigger: Prospect of Airbus launching a geared-turbofan re-engined A320
response: Committed to decide re-engine vs new airplane by end-2010

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we try to make these decisions in way where the current demand for current products is supported as we move into derivatives or all new airplanes. And we got a process in place that we don't think is going to cannibalize the demand we see now.
finding: Boeing times new-product decisions so they do not cannibalize demand for current products.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We wouldn't do it if they weren't ready. That's a big mistake in our business. So obviously, before we change the rate on the 777, we had in-depth discussions with our suppliers.
finding: Boeing makes supplier readiness a hard precondition before any rate change.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: As we have experienced in past cycles, the single-aisle market is leading the passenger recovery. This segment is showing the strongest growth, led by emerging markets and low-cost carriers. This growth, combined with our disciplined production and sales strategies, prompted our recently announced 737 production rate increase to 35 airplanes per month beginning in early 2012.
finding: Single-aisle demand from emerging markets and low-cost carriers led the recovery and prompted the 737 rate increase to 35/month in early 2012.
trigger: Single-aisle-led passenger recovery
response: 737 rate increase to 35/month from early 2012

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we will continue to assess the demand requirements in this growing market segment along with importantly, the ability of our supply chain to move to higher rates if warranted.
finding: Boeing tied any further 737 rate increase to two tests: market demand and supply-chain ability.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: This decision by the World's ruling body on trade matters is important for both Airbus and Boeing because it sets the precedent for emerging competitors from Canada, Brazil, China, Russia and others, who want to enter the market.
finding: Boeing used trade litigation against Airbus to set rules that would also constrain new entrants from Canada, Brazil, China and Russia.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: moving from where we've been, low 30s to something north of 35, puts a -- while your competitor is also looking at moves and while also other airplanes are also moving up in rate, can put pressure on suppliers.
finding: Boeing saw Airbus's parallel rate increases as competing for the same suppliers, making supplier capacity the binding limit on going above 35/month.
trigger: Airbus also raising narrowbody production rates
response: Methodical supplier-by-supplier readiness review before going above 35/month

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: If that is sometime this decade, then the case for re-engining weakens dramatically. If you did re-engine, you'd be doing two major developments in the course of four or five years, which makes no sense.
finding: Boeing's re-engine framework depended on when an all-new airplane became feasible; a new airplane this decade would make a 737 re-engine a wasteful second development.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: I think on balance, the customer feedback, which was your specific question, is sort of pushing us toward a newer airplane on balance. But there are those that also make the case for re-engining.
finding: In July 2010 Boeing read customer feedback as favoring a new airplane, while acknowledging a pro-re-engine camp.
trigger: Customer discussions at Farnborough 2010 on the 737 re-engine
response: Leaned toward a new airplane; decision due by year-end

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: understanding with clarity what the capabilities of the A350-1000 is or isn't is an important input to the 777 decision, and I think that is going to take some time. I mean I wouldn't totally characterize it as a paper airplane at this stage, but it's pretty close to that.
finding: Boeing tied its 777 upgrade decision to how the A350-1000's capabilities firmed up, which it treated as close to a paper airplane.
trigger: Airbus A350-1000 capability claims
response: Wait roughly a year for the A350-1000 configuration to firm before deciding on the 777

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: As you know, we have invested in additional capacity of our own in Charleston and some other places. So we do have some options to do some work ourselves if we can't reach the proper accommodation in some cases.
finding: Boeing kept its own capacity (such as Charleston) as a fallback for work it could not reach terms on with suppliers.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We have tremendous customer acceptance for what it does. We have plans to continue to upgrade them. And so the question would be, why re-engine? And the answer, in my view, is you would consider re-engineering if you weren't going to have an airplane available for another 10 to 15 years
finding: Boeing's default was to keep upgrading the accepted 737; it would re-engine only if a new airplane was 10-15 years away.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we recently announced our third 737 production rate increase this year to 38 airplanes per month beginning in the second quarter of 2013. This decision was supported by our current backlog of over 2,000 737s, existing options we expect customers to exercise and ongoing sales campaigns.
finding: Boeing justified its third 737 rate increase of 2010 (to 38/month) by a backlog of over 2,000 737s, expected option exercises and live sales campaigns.
trigger: Resurgence in air travel growth and strong customer demand
response: Third 737 rate increase of the year, to 38/month in 2Q 2013

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we see a new airplane opportunity out in the 220 range. And therefore, are continuing to question the necessity of a re-engine in the meantime, although we're studying it hard. And it is conceivable we would conclude that re-engining makes sense. But with the new airplane in the 2020 timeframe, it's not clear that it would.
finding: In October 2010 Boeing questioned whether a 737 re-engine was needed, given a possible new airplane around 2020, while studying it hard and not ruling it out.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: we are continuing to improve the 737. I mean, we've gotten 5% on fuel from the engines since we introduced the NG [ph], there's another 2% out ahead of us that we're introducing now. There's a new interior. So there's no reason to think that we wouldn't keep improving that, which also bears on the re-engine question.
finding: Instead of an immediate re-engine, Boeing defended the 737NG with incremental upgrades (5% fuel gain so far, 2% more coming, new interior), which it said bore on the re-engine decision.
trigger: Pressure to re-engine the 737 (Airbus A320 re-engine under study)
response: Incremental 737NG performance improvements while deferring the re-engine decision

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: if we do a new 737, roughly on 2020 timing, and as we're studying the market, that seems to be a timing that our customers might require. If we did a new narrow-body then we would probably have to address changes to the 777 before that.
finding: Boeing's sequencing: 777 changes first, then a new 737 around 2020, the timing it believed customers required.

speaker: Jim McNerney, CEO
quote: We're studying everything from a completely new airplane to modifications to the weighing in the engines. We're studying a wide range of options, and we're trying to figure out what our customers need.
finding: For the 777 Boeing kept options open, from an all-new airplane to re-engining and new-wing modifications, driven by customer needs.
